name: Battle of Nicopolis
info: An allied crusader army of French, Hungarians and others, with Venetian ships on the Danube, was routed by an Ottoman force under Bayezid I at Nicopolis in 1396, which ended the siege and left the Ottomans stronger in the Balkans.

facts.place: Before the fortress of Nicopolis on the lower Danube
facts.sides: A crusader army under King Sigismund of Hungary, with a French contingent nominally led by John, Count of Nevers, against an Ottoman force under Sultan Bayezid I. Numbers are heavily contested: 19th-century German historians reached about 7,500 to 15,000 Christians and about 12,000 to 20,000 Turks, while chroniclers give far higher figures.
facts.outcome: The crusaders were routed. Many were killed or captured, Sigismund escaped by boat, and the siege of Nicopolis was lifted.

t: The numbers are heavily contested: chroniclers give figures as high as 400,000 for the combatants, while 19th-century German historians estimated about 7,500 to 15,000 Christians and about 12,000 to 20,000 Turks.
The crusaders had no single commander. Sigismund's advice to let the Turkish vanguard be met by Wallachian foot soldiers was rejected by the French, who insisted on leading the charge.
After the defeat, Western Europe made no further move to stop the Turkish advance in the Balkans until the 1440s, and Constantinople fell in 1453.
dyk: The nearest thing to an eyewitness account was written by Johann Schiltberger, who was 16 when he saw the battle, was captured and spent 30 years enslaved by the Turks before he returned home and wrote it.
ev: After the Battle of Kosovo the Ottomans conquer most of the Balkans
Pope Boniface IX proclaims a new crusade against the Turks, and the Ottomans begin to blockade Constantinople
The crusade sets out from Dijon for Buda
The crusaders come within view of Nicopolis and begin the siege
The French charge, are met by Bayezid's reserve of sipahis, and the crusader army is routed
Bayezid has the prisoners brought before him, and many are executed while the nobles are spared for ransom
A ransom of 200,000 gold florins is agreed, and the noble prisoners are released on 24 June
Hungarians, Poles and Wallachians are defeated at the Battle of Varna

sections.background:
There were many minor crusades in the 14th century, undertaken by individual kings or knights, and the most recent, against Tunisia in 1390, had failed. After the Battle of Kosovo in 1389 the Ottomans had conquered most of the Balkans and reduced the Byzantine Empire to the area around Constantinople, which they blockaded from 1394. In 1393 the Bulgarian tsar Ivan Shishman had lost Nicopolis, his temporary capital, to the Ottomans, and his brother Ivan Stratsimir held Vidin as an Ottoman vassal. The Kingdom of Hungary had become the frontier between the two religions in Eastern Europe. Venice feared for its territories and its influence over the Adriatic, Ionian and Aegean seas, and Genoa feared an Ottoman monopoly of the trade routes to the Black Sea, where it had colonies.

In 1394 Pope Boniface IX proclaimed a new crusade, although the Western Schism had split the papacy between Avignon and Rome and the days when a pope could call a crusade were long past. Two factors decided its formation: a truce in the Hundred Years' War between Richard II's England and Charles VI's France, and the support of Philip II, Duke of Burgundy. Burgundy's interest lay chiefly in the prestige and power of himself and his house, and Barbara Tuchman notes that opulent display became the dominant theme, with plans, logistics and intelligence about the enemy coming second, if at all. A Hungarian delegation then reached Paris to ask for help on King Sigismund's behalf, and French nobles responded with enthusiasm.
sections.forces:
The number of combatants is heavily contested. Chroniclers give figures as high as 400,000, each side insisting that the enemy outnumbered it two to one. Tuchman dismisses the often-given figure of 100,000 crusaders, since so many men would have taken a month to cross the Danube at the Iron Gates and the crusaders took eight days. Johann Schiltberger, who saw the battle at the age of 16, put the crusaders at 17,000 and the Turks at 200,000. German historians of the 19th century reached about 7,500 to 15,000 Christians and about 12,000 to 20,000 Turks, noting that the countryside could not have fed scores of thousands of men and horses.

About 5,000 French knights and squires were said to have joined, with 6,000 archers and foot soldiers, some 11,000 men in all. The Knights Hospitaller of Rhodes came, Venice supplied ships, and Hungarian envoys encouraged German princes to join. Reports of 3,000 English knights, taken as fact by some historians, are doubted by others, since no English financial or royal preparations are recorded; Hospitallers of the English langue may account for mentions of the English. The Ottoman army is also estimated at 15,000 to 20,000, though some sources give up to 60,000. It included 1,500 Serbian heavy cavalry under Stefan Lazarević, Bayezid's brother-in-law and vassal.

Command was ambiguous. Philip of Burgundy, John of Gaunt and Louis of Orléans withdrew, and Burgundy named his 24-year-old son John, Count of Nevers, to nominal command, with the experienced Enguerrand de Coucy as chief counsellor. The French rules of March 1396 gave the Count and his company the vanguard.
sections.course:
The crusade left Dijon on 30 April 1396 and joined Sigismund at Buda. Philip's son Nevers had lingered at German courts and reached Vienna only on 24 June. At a war council in Buda, Sigismund advised letting the Turks make the long march to the crusaders, but the French rejected this. The army marched down the Danube, crossed at Orşova and took Vidin, whose ruler Stratsimir surrendered. At Oryahovo the inhabitants agreed to surrender to Sigismund, but the French broke the agreement, pillaging and massacring the town. On 12 September the crusaders reached Nicopolis. With no siege machines they settled down to starve the garrison out, and Bayezid marched quickly to its relief. On the 24th Sigismund proposed that Wallachian foot soldiers meet the Turkish vanguard, but the Constable d'Eu rejected this as demeaning to the knights, and prisoners taken at Oryahovo were massacred.

On 25 September the French vanguard, under d'Eu, rode out and crushed the untrained conscripts of the Turkish front line, though stakes hampered the horses. Coucy and Jean de Vienne urged a pause, but the younger knights pursued up the hill, many on foot. On the plateau they met a fresh corps of sipahis that Bayezid had kept in reserve. Vienne was killed, Nevers was taken prisoner, and the rest of the French yielded. Sipahis meanwhile swept down the flanks. The Transylvanians and Wallachians left the field, and the arrival of 1,500 Serbian knights proved critical against Sigismund's force. Sigismund and the Hospitaller Master escaped by boat to the Venetian ships.
sections.aftermath:
Sigismund later said to the Hospitaller Master, "We lost the day by the pride and vanity of these French." On 26 September Bayezid had the prisoners assembled. Jacques de Helly identified the chief nobles for ransom, among them Nevers, Coucy, Bar, d'Eu and La Tremoïlle, and those judged under 20 were taken as slaves. The rest, thought to number several thousand, were bound in groups and killed by decapitation or by the severing of limbs, while Nevers and the nobles watched. The killing lasted from early morning until late afternoon, when Bayezid called it off. The number of dead in the executions is said to have ranged from 300 to 3,000, and the number dead on the battlefield was much greater.

Few of those who fled survived. Men drowned swimming for the boats or the far bank, and those on board pushed away others trying to climb in. Sigismund sailed to the Black Sea and Constantinople and went home by sea. Survivors who crossed the Danube found the land already stripped by the Wallachians, and many starved. The captives were marched about 350 miles to Gallipoli and then taken to Bursa. News reached Paris in December, and Jacques de Helly rode in on Christmas. A ransom of 200,000 gold florins was agreed in June 1397. Coucy, d'Eu and others died in captivity or soon after, and the last of the leaders re-entered France in February 1398. A three-sided transaction between Burgundy, Sigismund and Venice took 27 years to settle.
sections.sources:
The closest record to a first-person account is by Johann Schiltberger, a German in the following of a Bavarian noble, who saw the battle at 16, was captured and was enslaved by the Turks for 30 years. He wrote a narrative after his return, but his figure for the Turks, 200,000, is wildly inflated. The Chronica Hungarorum, Jean Froissart, the Monk of St Denis and the poet Deschamps tell of the king's mood and of the grief in France, and the Ottoman historian Şükrullah, writing in the 1460s, gave 130,000 crusaders and 60,000 Ottomans. Medieval chroniclers had reasons to exaggerate: each side's numbers could comfort the losers or magnify the winners' glory.

Much is disputed. Tuchman writes that out of the welter of versions a coherent account of the movements on the field is not to be had. Chroniclers blamed the defeat on the crusaders' immorality, but Tuchman cautions that this was a contemporary tendency and cannot be verified. Gian Galeazzo Visconti was widely believed to have given Bayezid intelligence, though there is no firm evidence and he may have been a scapegoat. The English presence is doubted by some historians.
sections.legacy:
Nicopolis is often called the Crusade of Nicopolis, one of the last major crusades of the Middle Ages, together with the Crusade of Varna in 1443 to 1444. By their victory the Turks discouraged the formation of European coalitions against them. They maintained their pressure on Constantinople, tightened their control over the Balkans and became a greater threat to Central Europe. After the defeat, Western Europe made no further moves to stop the Turkish advance in the Balkans until the 1440s, and England and France soon renewed their war.

Wallachia continued its stance against the Ottomans, repelling expeditions in 1397 and 1400. In 1402 Bayezid was defeated and captured by Timur, and Mircea and the Kingdom of Hungary took advantage of the anarchy to campaign against the Ottomans. The Hungarians, Poles and Wallachians were defeated at the Battle of Varna in 1444, and Constantinople fell in 1453, followed by the Despotate of Morea in 1460, the Empire of Trebizond in 1461 and the Principality of Theodoro in 1475. The battle is also widely regarded as the end of the Second Bulgarian Empire, since hopes for its revival had come to an end, and its last ruler, Ivan Stratsimir, was captured and killed in Bursa.

Johan Huizinga remarked, with a historian's hindsight, on the lamentable consequences of statecraft recklessly embarking on an enterprise of vital import in the spirit of a chivalrous adventure, though participants and contemporary chroniclers did not analyse the event in these terms.

summary: At Nicopolis on 25 September 1396 a crusader army led by Sigismund of Hungary and a French contingent was routed by the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I, who then had many prisoners executed. The defeat ended the Second Bulgarian Empire and discouraged European coalitions against the Ottomans.
references: David Nicolle, Nicopolis 1396: The Last Crusade (Osprey Publishing, 1999)
Barbara W. Tuchman, A Distant Mirror: the Calamitous 14th Century (Alfred A. Knopf, 1978)
notes: Article spells Ivan Stratsimir's name as Stratsimir and Sratsimir; I used Stratsimir.

Numbers: the article says Schiltberger estimated crusaders at 17,000 and Turks at 200,000; German historians 7,500-15,000 and 12,000-20,000; Ottoman force 15-20,000 or up to 60,000; Sultan's execution toll 300-3,000.

The article says the French 'rules' of 28 March 1396 gave the Count the avant-garde; I wrote 'March 1396'. The crusaders' 'Hungarian delegation in August' lacks a year in the article (implied 1395); I left the year out.
I left out the Gian Galeazzo/Coucy diplomatic mission details, the Boucicaut scouting anecdote, and Coucy's ambush, for length.

The article names Ivan Shishman as tsar who lost Nicopolis in 1393 and Nicopolis as 'temporary capital'. Article says Nicopolis lies in Bulgaria only implicitly (Danubian fortress; Bulgarian tsar); the present-day country is not stated in the article.
